summary: We built Combustion Atlas, a public web dashboard that brings decades of NASA microgravity fire experiments into one place. NASA has run experiments like BASS, BASS-II, FLEX and Saffire for years, but the results are scattered across data tables and long technical reports with different formats and units, so it's hard to see what has already been tested. We combined the experiment tables with 29 NASA reports so you can ask a question and get an answer that quotes the original NASA pages word for word. You can also look up exact test conditions, and see on coverage heatmaps which oxygen and pressure conditions were tested, only planned, or never tested. Every value links back to its source, and anything uncertain is flagged instead of guessed. This matters because future spacecraft and habitats may use more oxygen than the ISS, and researchers need a fast, trustworthy way to find the gaps before planning the next fire-safety experiment.
details:
Fire is one of the most dangerous emergencies on a spacecraft, and it behaves differently in microgravity. Without gravity, flames turn round, spread slowly and can keep burning at oxygen levels that would put them out on Earth. NASA has studied this for decades through experiments like BASS, BASS-II, FLEX and Saffire. The results are spread across data tables and long technical reports with different formats and units, so before planning a new experiment, a researcher has to dig through all of it just to find out what's already been tested.

Combustion Atlas brings that evidence into one place. You can ask questions in plain English and get answers that quote the original NASA pages, with numbered footnotes. Coverage heatmaps show which oxygen and pressure conditions were tested, which were only planned, and which were never tested. A 3-D evidence map shows where the research is deep and where it's thin. It's built for fire-safety researchers, spacecraft designers, mission planners and students.

We combined 546 experiment runs from NASA's PSI repository with 29 NASA documents. An AI model helped transcribe the tables, and we reviewed the flagged values by hand. Uncertain values keep a visible note instead of a guessed number. The chat uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and our code checks every quote and number against the source before an answer is shown. The site runs on Python and FastAPI with a React front end, is hosted on Microsoft Azure, and is open source on GitHub.

Future Moon and Mars habitats may use more oxygen than the ISS does, and those are the conditions that are barely tested. Combustion Atlas helps researchers spot those gaps quickly and plan the next experiment with evidence they can trust.
